summary:
The name of the bill is "Mines and Minerals Act, 2083" (Section 1, Subsection 1, Page 1). The main purpose of this bill is to manage geo-scientific study, research, and exploration and excavation of mines and minerals, and to develop, promote, and regulate mineral-based industries (Preamble, Page 1). This Act shall come into force on the ninety-first day from the date of authentication (Section 1, Subsection 2, Page 1).

According to this bill, all mineral substances existing in a natural state on the surface of the land or underground shall be the property of the Government of Nepal (Section 3, Page 2). The Government of Nepal shall have the right to excavate mines and minerals, and may carry out excavation itself or through companies by granting permission (Section 5, Subsection 1, Subsection 2, Page 3). The Government of Nepal may, by publishing a notice in the Nepal Gazette, designate mines and minerals to be excavated by provincial governments and local levels (Section 5, Subsection 4, Page 3). The Government of Nepal shall protect minerals designated by it, may declare strategic or tactical minerals, declare mineral areas, and restrict exports or sales (Section 6, Subsection 2, Page 3; Section 7, Subsection 1, Page 3; Section 8, Subsection 1, Page 4; Section 26, Page 12). Provincial governments shall have the right to explore mines and minerals in accordance with provincial law (Section 4, Subsection 1, Page 2). Exploration of minerals spreading across two or more provinces shall be done by mutual consent or through the Department upon request to the Government of Nepal (Section 4, Subsection 2, Subsection 3, Page 2-3). Local levels must protect mines and minerals located within their geographical territory (Section 6, Subsection 1, Page 3). Local levels shall receive ten percent of the royalty as a local mineral utilization fee (Section 52, Subsection 2, Page 20). The federal, provincial, and local levels must coordinate with one another when operating mineral activities (Section 28, Subsection 1, Subsection 2, Subsection 3, Page 12).

Companies wanting to explore or excavate mineral substances must obtain an exploration or excavation license from the licensing authority (Section 11, Subsection 1, Page 4). Applications for exploration licenses under federal jurisdiction must be submitted to the Department in the prescribed format (Section 12, Subsection 2, Page 5). Applications for extending exploration licenses must be submitted at least forty-five days before the expiry of the license (Section 13, Subsection 2, Page 5). Applications for excavation licenses must be submitted to the designated body along with a work plan at least forty-five days before the expiry of the exploration license (Section 14, Subsection 1, Page 5-6). Applications for extending excavation licenses must be submitted with a technical report three months before expiry (Section 15, Subsection 2, Page 6). Excavation license-holding companies may reapply with a work plan one year before expiry (Section 15, Subsection 4, Page 7). For license renewal, applications must be submitted within forty-five days after the end of each fiscal year attached with renewal fees and proof of land rent payment, or within an additional fifteen days by paying double fees (Section 17, Subsection 1, Subsection 2, Page 8). License-holding companies must begin exploration within six months from the date of obtaining an exploration license and begin excavation within two years from the date of obtaining an excavation license (Section 19, Subsection 1, Page 9). Applications for extension must be submitted ninety days before expiry (Section 19, Subsection 2, Page 9). If other minerals are discovered, applications must be submitted within thirty days (Section 22, Subsection 2, Page 10). Companies must comply with environmental laws and mitigate impacts (Section 24, Subsection 1, Subsection 2, Page 10). Reports must be submitted within seven days of starting exploration and within thirty days of starting excavation (Section 29, Subsection 1, Page 12). Annual reports must be submitted within forty-five days after the end of each fiscal year (Section 29, Subsection 2, Page 12). Within one year of completing excavation, companies must physically restore the excavation area and submit an integrated final report (Section 29, Subsection 3, Page 12). If strategic, tactical, or radioactive minerals are found, immediate notice must be given to the Department (Section 32, Page 14). Companies must pay land rent for each fiscal year as per Schedule-4, deposit security as per Schedule-3, and pay royalty as per Schedule-5 before exporting excavated minerals (Section 50, Subsection 1, Page 19; Section 51, Page 19; Section 52, Subsection 1, Page 19-20). Prior approval must be obtained when selling or transferring shares/ownership or changing the company name (Section 46, Subsection 1, Page 18).

The duration of exploration licenses shall be three years for precious minerals, two years for important minerals, and one year for common minerals (Section 13, Subsection 1, Page 5). The term of an exploration license may be extended once for one year (Section 13, Subsection 3, Page 5). The duration of excavation licenses shall be ten years for ultra-small scale, fifteen years for small scale, twenty years for medium scale, and thirty years for large scale (Section 15, Subsection 1, Page 6). The term of an excavation license may be extended once for two years for ultra-small scale, three years for small scale, five years for medium scale, and seven years for large scale (Section 15, Subsection 3, Page 7). While the excavation license process is ongoing, a temporary extension may be granted for up to three years, not exceeding one year at a time (Section 14, Subsection 8, Page 6; Section 15, Subsection 5, Page 7).
